instrument.full_name: Declaration concerning the Prohibition of the Use of Projectiles the Sole Object of which is the Diffusion of Asphyxiating or Deleterious Gases
instrument.adopted_at: The Hague, First International Peace Conference (question raised in the First Commission's second (naval) subcommission, voted in the First Commission, adopted in plenary, and embodied in a separate act listed in the Final Act of 29 July 1899)
instrument.depositary: Government of the Netherlands. Ratifications are deposited at The Hague (operative para. 5), adhesions and denunciations are notified to the Netherlands Government (operative paras. 7 and 8), and the single original is kept in its archives (closing formula).
instrument.key_non_parties: The United States neither signed nor ratified: Captain Mahan voted against the prohibition in the subcommission, the First Commission and (with Great Britain) in plenary (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 79, 284, 329, 366-367); the Dutch royal order of 23 January 1905 (FRUS 1905, doc. 704) marks the United States "neither signed nor ratified"; the depositary database and the ICRC list no United States entry; and Bevans, vol. 1, lists only Hague I to III and IV,1 among the acts of 29 July 1899. Great Britain voted against in 1899 and did not sign, but adhered on 30 August 1907 (Scott 1915, p. 226; Trb. 1966, 232). Most present-day states are not listed as parties; the depositary database lists 35 (checked 12 October 2026).
instrument.duration_clause: No term is stated. The undertaking to abstain (operative para. 1) is given without limit of time, unlike the five-year term of the sister Declaration (IV,1) on balloons. Its application in a particular war depends on the general participation clause (operative paras. 2 and 3). The depositary records entry into force on 4 September 1900 and no termination.
instrument.withdrawal_clause: A High Contracting Party may denounce the Declaration by written notification to the Netherlands Government, which communicates it forthwith to the other Contracting Powers; the denunciation takes effect one year after the notification (operative para. 8) and affects only the notifying Power (operative para. 9). The engagement also ceases to be binding in a particular war once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3); that is a condition of application, not withdrawal. No denunciation is recorded in the depositary database.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: Ratification "as soon as possible" (operative para. 4), with ratifications deposited at The Hague and a proces-verbal drawn up on each deposit (operative paras. 5 and 6). The text sets no threshold and no entry-into-force date. The Netherlands Treaty Series (Trb. 1966, 232, section G) records that the Declaration entered into force on 4 September 1900 for the states that had ratified by that date and, for later ratifying or acceding states, on the dates of their deposit or accession. Non-signatory Powers may adhere by written notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7); the text does not say when an adhesion takes effect.
instrument.count_basis: The Declaration has no numbered articles. Citations use: preamble (the paragraphs from "The undersigned" to the reference to the St Petersburg Declaration); operative paras. 1 to 9 (the paragraphs after "Declare as follows", namely 1 prohibition, 2 binding only between Contracting Powers, 3 cessation when a non-contracting Power joins, 4 ratification, 5 deposit at The Hague, 6 proces-verbal, 7 adhesion, 8 denunciation, 9 effect of denunciation); and the closing formula. The Netherlands Treaty Series uses the same count ("alinea 5" for ratification, "alinea 7" for accession). Word count: authentic French text as reproduced by the ICRC (French page), from "Les soussignés" to the end of the dating formula, excluding the title and "(Signatures)", whitespace tokenization with elided forms (e.g. d'être) counted as one word and the detached colon after "Déclarent" not counted: 308. The same procedure gives 318 for Declaration IV,1, the figure recorded there. Scott, Les Conventions et Déclarations de La Haye (1918), pp. 225-226, prints the St Petersburg date as "29 Novembre/11 Décembre", which gives 307 on the same basis. English: the local Avalon PDF (Scott translation), from "The Undersigned" to the end of the dating formula: 319.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Projectiles the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases. In the subcommission the President defined the proposal as covering projectiles whose purpose is to spread asphyxiating gases, not those whose explosion incidentally produces such gases (Proceedings, 1899, p. 366).
instrument.key_provisions: The Contracting Powers agree to abstain from the use of projectiles the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases (operative para. 1). The Declaration binds only Contracting Powers in a war between two or more of them (operative para. 2) and ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3). It is subject to ratification, with deposit at The Hague (operative paras. 4 to 6); non-signatory Powers may adhere by notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7); denunciation takes effect one year after written notification and affects only the notifying Power (operative paras. 8 and 9). The preamble invokes the sentiments of the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration.
instrument.behavior_change: Delegates described the prohibited projectiles as not yet existing; on that account, the restriction concerned a prospective capability rather than an identified fielded weapon. In the First Commission on 22 June 1899 Captain Mahan (United States) said that projectiles of this kind "do not really exist", and the Danish delegate, Mr Bille, said there was no occasion to discuss a projectile which does not exist when Russia and Germany had said that present means of warfare were more than sufficient (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 283-284). In the subcommission on 31 May the British delegate thought such an invention unlikely (p. 367). During the First World War Germany fired irritant-filled shells in 1914 and January 1915 that also carried shrapnel or explosive, so that their "sole" purpose was not gas, and released chlorine from cylinders at Ypres on 22 April 1915, as reported by Tucker (2006).
instrument.historical_background: Russia's circular of 30 December 1898 (11 January 1899, new style) proposed, as point 2, banning new explosives more powerful than those in use (Scott 1915, pp. xvi-xvii). In the First Commission's naval subcommission on 31 May 1899 the Russian naval delegate, Captain Scheine, proposed prohibiting projectiles that spread asphyxiating or deleterious gases; most delegates agreed on condition of unanimity, the United States voted against and Siam reserved its vote. The First Commission adopted the prohibition on 22 June against the single vote of the United States, and on 20 July by 17 votes to 2 (United States and Great Britain). The plenary Conference adopted it on 21 July with the same two votes against, and 16 Powers signed the Declaration at the closing meeting on 29 July 1899 (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 79, 221, 283-284, 328-329, 365-367).

provisions.provision: Prohibit use of projectiles whose sole object is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power on identical terms ("The Contracting Powers agree to abstain")
provisions.geographic_scope: No geographic limit; applies in a war between two or more Contracting Powers
provisions.exceptions: Binding only in a war between two or more Contracting Powers (operative para. 2); ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3). The word "sole" limits the rule to projectiles whose only object is gas diffusion: in the subcommission the President defined the proposal as excluding projectiles whose explosion incidentally produces gases (Proceedings, 1899, p. 366), and on 17 July Captains Mahan and Scheine said the word had been inserted purposely (p. 326). The text does not address gas released other than by projectiles.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: The Contracting Powers agree to abstain from the use of projectiles the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases.
provisions.locator: Operative para. 1 (French: "Les Puissances contractantes s'interdisent l'emploi de projectiles qui ont pour but unique de répandre des gaz asphyxiants ou délétères."). Entry into force from the Netherlands treaty database (4 September 1900); no termination recorded.

events.event: Russian circular proposes banning new explosives
events.attribution: Circular printed in Scott, The Hague Conventions and Declarations of 1899 and 1907 (1915)
events.description: The second Russian circular listed the subjects for the conference. Point 2 proposed the "interdiction of the employment in armies and fleets of new firearms of every description and of new explosives". The gas proposal was later raised under this point in the naval subcommission.

events.event: Naval subcommission debates a ban on asphyxiating-gas projectiles
events.actors: Second subcommission of the First Commission; Russia (Captain Scheine); United States (Captain Mahan); Great Britain (Admiral Sir John Fisher); Siam
events.attribution: Minutes of the second subcommission, third meeting, and its report (Count Soltyk), in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Captain Scheine proposed prohibiting projectiles that spread asphyxiating and deleterious gases; the President, Jonkheer van Karnebeek, defined the proposal as covering projectiles whose purpose is to spread such gases, not those whose explosion incidentally produces them. France, Austria-Hungary, Sweden and Norway, Japan, the Netherlands, Denmark, Turkey, Italy and Germany answered yes on condition of unanimity, and the British delegate favoured the prohibition. Mahan voted no and had his reasons entered in the minutes; Siam reserved its vote. The subcommission report counts 14 representatives in favour on condition of unanimity.
events.locator: Second subcommission, third meeting, pp. 365-367; report, pp. 295-296

events.event: First Commission adopts the prohibition against one vote
events.actors: First Commission; United States (Captain Mahan); Netherlands (Jonkheer van Karnebeek); Russia (Captain Scheine)
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, third meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Mahan maintained his negative vote, saying such projectiles did not really exist and that asphyxiating enemies with gas was no more cruel than drowning them when a torpedo sinks a vessel. Van Karnebeek replied that the matter should also be seen from the standpoint of land war and the danger to non-combatants in a siege; Scheine compared gas to poisoning a river. The prohibition was adopted unanimously except for the United States; Germany, Austria-Hungary, Great Britain, Italy, Japan and Portugal accepted it only on condition of unanimity.

events.event: First Commission debates the draft report and the word "sole"
events.actors: First Commission; United States (Captain Mahan); Russia (Captain Scheine); Germany (Captain Siegel); Great Britain (Sir Julian Pauncefote); Portugal (Count de Macedo)
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, seventh meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The reporter's proposal to extend the St Petersburg Declaration to the three points for five years was dropped after objections, including from Mahan and Scheine that a five-year term would change the scope of the gas and bullet votes. Siegel and Pauncefote recorded that many affirmative gas votes had been conditional on unanimity. De Macedo thought the word "sole" had been inserted by mistake; Mahan and Scheine said it had been inserted purposely.

events.event: First Commission votes 17 to 2 on the gas prohibition
events.actors: First Commission; United States (Captain Mahan); Great Britain
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, eighth meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The reporter appealed to the United States delegation to withdraw its negative vote. Mahan, speaking for the delegation, said it did not deem it logical to permit submarine boats and prohibit shells filled with asphyxiating gases, and could not reverse a vote of principle. De Macedo said he had voted yes although he thought the word "sole" took all force from the prohibition. The Commission decided to propose a separate declaration or convention on each point and adopted the gas point by 17 votes to 2 (United States and Great Britain).

events.event: Plenary Conference adopts the gas engagement
events.actors: Plenary Conference (reporter Jonkheer van Karnebeek); United States; Great Britain
events.attribution: Minutes of the sixth plenary meeting and annexed report, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The engagement prohibiting the use of projectiles which have for their sole end the spreading of asphyxiating or deleterious gases was "adopted unanimously less two votes (United States of America and Great Britain)". The Commission's report to the Conference noted that six affirmative votes had been cast only on condition of unanimity.
events.locator: Sixth plenary meeting, p. 79; report, p. 88

events.event: Plenary adopts the final texts and signature arrangements
events.actors: Plenary Conference; Drafting Committee (reporter Louis Renault)
events.attribution: Minutes of the seventh and eighth plenary meetings, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: On 25 July the Conference approved the Final Act, under which the Conventions and the three Declarations form separate acts, dated the day of signature, which may be signed until 31 December 1899. On 27 July Renault presented the common preamble and final clauses, explaining that the reference to St Petersburg did not imply adhesion to the 1868 Declaration, and the Conference adopted the texts.
events.locator: Seventh plenary meeting, p. 103; eighth plenary meeting, pp. 211-212

events.event: Declaration adopted and signed at The Hague
events.actors: Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, France, Greece, Mexico, Montenegro, Netherlands, Persia, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Siam, Spain, Sweden and Norway, Turkey
events.attribution: Table of signatures read at the closing meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920); Netherlands treaty database; ICRC
events.description: The Declaration is dated 29 July 1899, the date of the Final Act. The table of signatures read at the closing meeting lists 16 Powers as having signed it that day. The United States and Great Britain did not sign.
events.locator: Closing meeting, p. 221 (page inferred from neighbouring running heads); text and signature blocks, pp. 266-267

events.event: Signature open until 31 December 1899
events.attribution: Final Act, as reported at the seventh plenary meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Under the Final Act the Declaration could be signed until 31 December 1899 by the plenipotentiaries of the Powers represented. Austria-Hungary, China, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the Kingdom of Serbia and Switzerland are not in the closing-meeting list but appear as signatories in the 1899 table of signatures to 31 December and in the depositary record, which gives every signature the date of the act; their actual signature dates were not established.
events.locator: Seventh plenary meeting, p. 103; table of signatures, p. 268

events.event: First deposit of ratifications and entry into force
events.actors: Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Persia, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Siam, Spain, Sweden and Norway
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; Netherlands Treaty Series (Trb. 1966, 232); ICRC
events.description: The depositary and the ICRC give entry into force on 4 September 1900. Trb. 1966, 232 states that the provisions entered into force on that date for the states that had ratified by then. The ICRC gives Denmark and Spain 4 November 1900; the depositary database, Trb. 1966, 232, the 1905 Dutch royal order and Scott (1915) give 4 September 1900.
events.locator: Treaty data: entry into force 04-09-1900; Trb. 1966, 232, sections E and G

events.event: China deposits its ratification
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; ICRC; Dutch royal order of 23 January 1905 (FRUS 1905)
events.description: China's ratification was deposited on 21 November 1904, the last by a signatory other than Turkey.

events.event: Dutch royal order publishes the list of ratifications
events.actors: Netherlands (Queen Wilhelmina; Foreign Minister Melvil van Lynden)
events.attribution: Royal order of 23 January 1905 (Staatsblad 1905, no. 29), translation enclosed in a despatch from the United States chargé at The Hague, FRUS 1905
events.description: The order lists the Powers for which the 1899 acts were obligatory on 31 December 1904. For Declaration IV,2 it lists 23 ratifying Powers, including Montenegro (16 October 1900); it marks Great Britain and the United States as having neither signed nor ratified and Turkey as having signed but not ratified.

events.event: Norway and Sweden listed as parties by succession
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database (parties table)
events.description: The depositary database lists Norway and Sweden separately with consent type "Su" (succession) and entry into force on 17 June 1905, beside the entry for the Kingdom of Sweden and Norway. The basis of the entries and their date were not established; Scott (1915) and the 1905 royal order list only Sweden and Norway.

events.event: Turkey deposits its ratification
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; Trb. 1966, 232; Scott (1915)
events.description: Turkey, which had signed on 29 July 1899, deposited its ratification on 12 June 1907, completing ratification by all signatory Powers (Scott 1915, p. 226).

events.event: Great Britain adheres
events.attribution: Scott (1915); Trb. 1966, 232; Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Great Britain, which had voted against the prohibition in 1899 and did not sign, adhered under operative para. 7 on 30 August 1907. The depositary database lists the entry as an accession by the United Kingdom.

events.event: Nicaragua adheres
events.attribution: Scott (1915); Trb. 1966, 232; Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Nicaragua adhered under operative para. 7 on 11 October 1907.

events.event: German chlorine release at Ypres
events.attribution: Reported by Tucker, War of Nerves (2006), excerpt published by NPR
events.description: Germany released about 168 tonnes of chlorine from 5,730 cylinders against French and Algerian troops near Langemarck. Tucker reports that the German High Command read the Declaration as banning only shells designed specifically to release lethal gas, and that Fritz Haber noted that release from cylinders would not technically violate it. Tucker also reports earlier French use of tear-gas grenades from August 1914 and German irritant shells, combined with shrapnel or explosive, at Neuve-Chapelle (October 1914) and Bolimow (January 1915).

events.event: Sir John French alleges defiance of the Hague Convention
events.actors: United Kingdom (Field Marshal Sir John French); Germany
events.attribution: Despatch of 15 June 1915 to the Secretary of State for War, published in the London Gazette (second supplement of 10 July 1915), transcribed by The Long, Long Trail
events.description: French wrote that the enemy's fighting had been characterised by "a cynical and barbarous disregard of the well-known usages of civilised war and a flagrant defiance of the Hague Convention", referring to the use of poisonous gas from 22 April 1915. The despatch does not name Declaration IV,2. No formal finding on this Declaration was identified in the sources reviewed.

events.event: United States enters the war
events.attribution: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State, Milestones
events.description: The House of Representatives concurred in the declaration of war on Germany two days after the Senate vote of 4 April 1917. The United States was not a party to the Declaration (FRUS 1905, doc. 704; depositary database). Under operative para. 3 the Declaration ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins a belligerent; no source reviewed was found that applies this clause to the war after April 1917.
events.locator: U.S. Entry into World War I, 1917

events.event: Geneva Protocol on gases signed
events.attribution: Text of the Protocol, ICRC IHL Databases
events.description: The Protocol's preamble records that the prohibition of the use in war of asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases "has been declared in Treaties to which the majority of Powers of the world are Parties", and its parties accept the prohibition "so far as they are not already Parties to Treaties prohibiting such use". Any relationship to this Declaration is coded on the 1925 record.

events.event: Ethiopia adheres
events.attribution: Trb. 1966, 232; Netherlands treaty database; ICRC
events.description: Ethiopia adhered under operative para. 7 on 9 August 1935. Italy, an original party, invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 and used chemical weapons, chiefly sulphur mustard; Grip and Hart (SIPRI, 2009) describe the legal debate at the League of Nations within the framework of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. No allegation framed under this Declaration was identified in the sources reviewed.
events.locator: Section F; SIPRI (2009), sections I and V

events.event: Soviet Union recognises the Hague Declarations ratified by Russia
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database (declaration text); Trb. 1981, 94
events.description: The USSR recognised the 1899 and 1907 Hague Conventions and Declarations ratified by Russia to the extent that they do not conflict with the UN Charter and have not been amended or superseded by later agreements to which the USSR is a party, "such as the 1925 Geneva Protocol". The depositary records the entry under the Russian Federation.

events.event: Ukraine confirms succession
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Ukraine confirmed the validity for it, by succession from 24 August 1991, of the 1899 and 1907 Hague Conventions and Declarations recognised by the USSR in the format and scope of the Soviet note of 7 March 1955. The depositary circulated the notification on 10 June 2015.
events.locator: Reservations and declarations: Ukraine; notification Conventions 1899 A 05 No. 01/2015

participation.notes: Netherlands treaty database (depositary): signature 29-07-1899, ratification (R) and entry into force 1900-09-04, no termination. Not in the list of 16 Powers that signed at the closing meeting on 29 July 1899 (Proceedings, 1899, p. 221); the Final Act left signature open until 31 December 1899. overview_md: The Hague Declaration (IV,2) of 29 July 1899 commits its parties to abstain from the use of projectiles the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases ([ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-2-1899)). It was one of three declarations adopted at the First Hague Peace Conference, alongside those on balloons and expanding bullets. Twenty-four Powers signed it (counting Sweden and Norway once) and all of them had ratified by 1907; Great Britain and Nicaragua adhered in 1907 and Ethiopia in 1935 ([Trb. 1966, 232](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1966-232.pdf)). The United States neither signed nor ratified. The Declaration binds only in wars between parties and ceases to bind once a non-party joins a belligerent. It entered into force on 4 September 1900 and has no fixed term; the depositary and the ICRC treat it as in force, and the depositary database lists 35 present-day parties, several of them by succession ([Netherlands treaty database](https://treatydatabase.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/002422_p.html)). Its narrow wording was tested in the First World War, when Germany released chlorine from cylinders rather than projectiles, and the 1925 Geneva Protocol later stated a prohibition on the use in war of asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases.
provisions_md:
The Declaration has no numbered articles. Citations refer to the preamble, nine operative paragraphs and the closing formula of the [authentic French text](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/fr/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-2-1899/declaration), checked against [Scott, Les Conventions et Déclarations de La Haye (1918)](https://archive.org/details/lesconventionset00laha), pp. 225-226; the [English translation](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-2-1899/declaration) follows the same order.

### Preamble
- The plenipotentiaries declare themselves inspired by the sentiments expressed in the St Petersburg Declaration of 29 November (11 December) 1868. Louis Renault told the Conference that this wording did not imply adhesion to the 1868 Declaration ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), p. 211).

### The prohibition
- The Contracting Powers agree to abstain from the use of projectiles the sole object of which is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases (operative para. 1).
- The word "sole" limits the rule. In the naval subcommission the President defined the proposal as covering projectiles whose purpose is to spread such gases, not those whose explosion incidentally produces them (Proceedings, p. 366). Captains Mahan and Scheine said the word was inserted purposely; the Portuguese delegate, Count de Macedo, considered that it took all force from the prohibition (pp. 326 and 328).
- The rule concerns use in war by projectiles. The text does not address gas released by other means, nor the development, production or possession of gas munitions.

### Bound parties and the general participation clause
- The Declaration binds Contracting Powers identically, but only in a war between two or more of them (operative para. 2).
- It ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3).

### Duration
- No term is stated; the obligation is not time-limited, unlike the five-year balloon Declaration (IV,1) signed the same day.

### Final clauses
- Ratification as soon as possible, deposit at The Hague, and a proces-verbal of each deposit sent to all Contracting Powers (operative paras. 4 to 6).
- Non-signatory Powers may adhere by written notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7).
- Denunciation takes effect one year after written notification to the Netherlands Government and affects only the notifying Power (operative paras. 8 and 9).
- The text contains no provisions on information exchange, verification, consultation, dispute settlement or enforcement.
participation_md:
- **Signature.** The Declaration is dated 29 July 1899. Sixteen Powers signed at the closing meeting that day; under the Final Act signature remained open until 31 December 1899, and eight more Powers appear as signatories ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), pp. 103, 221 and 268). Their actual signature dates were not established; the depositary records all signatures under 29 July 1899.
- **Ratification and entry into force.** Ratifications were deposited at The Hague. The Declaration entered into force on 4 September 1900 for the Powers that had ratified by then and later for each subsequent ratifying or acceding state on its date of deposit or accession ([Trb. 1966, 232](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1966-232.pdf)). Turkey was the last signatory to ratify, on 12 June 1907.
- **Adhesion.** Open to non-signatory Powers (operative para. 7). Great Britain (30 August 1907), Nicaragua (11 October 1907) and Ethiopia (9 August 1935) adhered.
- **Succession.** The [depositary database](https://treatydatabase.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/002422_p.html) lists entries by succession for Austria and Hungary (1918), Norway and Sweden (1905), India and Pakistan (1950), Fiji (1973), South Africa (1978), Serbia (2001), Montenegro (2007) and Ukraine (2015), and records declarations by the USSR (1955) and Belarus (1962) recognising the Hague acts ratified by Russia, subject to conditions ([Trb. 1981, 94](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1981-94.pdf)).
- **Participants.** 24 signatories, all of which ratified (counting Sweden and Norway once). The depositary database lists 35 present-day parties, checked 12 October 2026; the [ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-2-1899/state-parties) lists 33, without India and Pakistan. Neither the current depositary database nor the ICRC lists Montenegro's 1900 ratification, which appears in Trb. 1966, 232 and the 1905 Dutch list ([FRUS 1905, doc. 704](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1905/d704)). The United States is not a party.
- **Duration.** No term; in force according to the depositary and the ICRC.
- **Withdrawal.** Denunciation on one year's written notice to the Netherlands Government (operative paras. 8 and 9); none recorded.
- **Amendment and review.** No amendment procedure and no review conferences.
- **Depositary.** The Government of the Netherlands.
history_md:
### Origins
Russia's circular of 30 December 1898 (11 January 1899, new style) proposed banning new explosives more powerful than those in use ([Scott 1915](https://archive.org/details/hagueconventions00inteuoft), pp. xvi-xvii). In the First Commission's naval subcommission on 31 May 1899 the Russian naval delegate, Captain Scheine, proposed prohibiting projectiles that spread asphyxiating and deleterious gases, which he called barbarous and equivalent to poisoning a river ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), pp. 365-366).

### Negotiation
At the same meeting Captain A. T. Mahan of the United States voted no and had his reasons entered in the minutes: the charge of barbarity had been made against every new weapon, it had not been shown that gas projectiles would not produce a decisive result, and his country should not deprive itself by hasty resolutions of means that might later be useful (pp. 366-367). On 16 June he had the record amended to read "cruel without being decisive" (p. 375). Most naval delegates agreed on condition of unanimity; Siam reserved its vote (p. 296). In the First Commission on 22 June Mahan said such projectiles did not really exist and that asphyxiation by gas was no more cruel than drowning a ship's crew by torpedo; Jonkheer van Karnebeek and Captain Scheine disputed the comparison, and the Danish delegate, Mr Bille, said there was no occasion to discuss a projectile which does not exist when Russia and Germany had stated that present means of warfare were more than sufficient. The prohibition was adopted against the United States vote alone, with Germany, Austria-Hungary, Great Britain, Italy, Japan and Portugal accepting it only on condition that it be adopted unanimously (pp. 283-284). On 20 July Mahan declined to change his vote, saying it was not logical to permit submarine boats while prohibiting gas shells, and the Commission voted 17 to 2, Great Britain joining the United States (pp. 328-329). The plenary Conference adopted the engagement on 21 July with the same two votes against (p. 79), and 16 Powers signed on 29 July (p. 221).

### Participation
All 24 signatories ratified by 1907; Great Britain adhered on 30 August 1907 ([Scott 1915](https://archive.org/details/hagueconventions00inteuoft), p. 226). The United States remained outside ([FRUS 1905](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1905/d704)).

### First World War
Tucker reports that the German High Command read the Declaration as covering only shells designed specifically to release gas, and that Fritz Haber noted that releasing chlorine from cylinders would not technically violate it; Germany did so at Ypres on 22 April 1915 ([Tucker 2006](https://www.npr.org/2006/05/08/5391044/excerpt-war-of-nerves)). In a despatch dated 15 June 1915 Field Marshal Sir John French alleged "a flagrant defiance of the Hague Convention", without naming this Declaration ([despatch](https://www.longlongtrail.co.uk/battles/british-field-commanders-despatches/sir-john-frenchs-eighth-despatch-second-ypres-aubers-and-festubert/)). The United States, a non-party, entered the war in April 1917 ([Office of the Historian](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1914-1920/wwi)); no source reviewed applies operative para. 3 to that event, and no formal finding under the Declaration was identified.

### Later record
The [1925 Geneva Protocol](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/geneva-gas-prot-1925) recalls that the prohibition had been declared in earlier treaties and binds parties not already bound by them. Ethiopia adhered in August 1935; the legal debate over Italy's use of mustard gas in 1935-36 was conducted under the Geneva Protocol ([Grip and Hart, SIPRI 2009](https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/Italo-Ethiopian-war.pdf)). The USSR's 1955 recognition of the Hague acts was qualified by reference to the Geneva Protocol ([Netherlands treaty database](https://treatydatabase.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/002422_p.html)).

coding_notes.note: Coded Declaration, the parties' own title. The text is an engagement subject to ratification and denunciation, deposited with the Netherlands Government.

Legally binding, from the text (an engagement "binding" on the Contracting Powers, operative para. 2, subject to ratification and denunciation, operative paras. 4 to 9) and its publication in the Netherlands Treaty Series.

In force: the depositary database records entry into force on 4 September 1900 and no termination (status "Inwerkinggetreden"), and the ICRC records the Declaration as in force. The text has no term. Later instruments, notably the 1925 Geneva Protocol, are described in prose and coded on their own records.

29 July 1899, the date of the Final Act and of the Declaration, also given by the ICRC as the date of adoption. The plenary Conference adopted the engagement on 21 July and the final text on 27 July 1899; those votes are recorded as events. The Final Act, which lists this Declaration as a separate act, is treated as the conference's adoption act.
29 July 1899. Under the Final Act the separate acts could be signed until 31 December 1899 (Proceedings, 1899, p. 103), so an Opening for signature event is recorded.

4 September 1900 from the Netherlands treaty database, the ICRC and Trb. 1966, 232; the text has no entry-into-force clause. Later ratifying, acceding and succeeding states became bound on the dates the depositary records.

35, checked 12 October 2026 against the depositary database (XML last modified 23 June 2022): every entry without a termination date, excluding the three historical entries Austria/Hungary, Kingdom of Sweden and Norway, and "Yugoslavia (< 25-06-1991)" (the Kingdom of Serbia's 1899 signature and 1901 ratification). The 35 current entries, reconciled one to one with the Participation rows marked State Party: Austria, Belarus, Belgium, Bulgaria, China, Denmark, Ethiopia, Fiji, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, India, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, Montenegro, Netherlands, Nicaragua, Norway, Pakistan, Persia, Portugal, Romania, Russian Federation, Serbia, Siam, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, Ukraine, United Kingdom (Persia and Siam appear in the depositary as Iran and Thailand). They comprise 20 original signatories, 3 accessions (United Kingdom, Nicaragua, Ethiopia) and 12 successions. Montenegro (1878-1918) is not counted. The ICRC lists 33, without India and Pakistan. The count reports the depositary's current listing; for states listed under a modern name (Germany, Iran, the Russian Federation, Thailand, Türkiye, China) it does not code continuity with the Power that signed.

24, counting Sweden and Norway once: the 16 Powers that signed at the closing meeting and 8 that signed later in 1899 (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 221 and 268). The current depositary database shows 23 signature entries because it omits Montenegro's 1899 participation; the ICRC shows 25 signature entries because it lists Austria and Hungary, and Norway and Sweden, separately and omits Montenegro.
Chemical weapons: the rule concerns projectiles whose sole object is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases.
Not specific: the text sets no environmental limit. The question was raised in the naval subcommission and discussed for both naval and land warfare (Proceedings, 1899, p. 283).

The attached reading text is the ICRC English translation, checked against the English text in the Proceedings (1899), p. 266. Produced by the First Hague Peace Conference (AC-78). Negotiated alongside the other five acts of 29 July 1899 (AC-85, AC-82, AC-83, AC-84, AC-81), which the Final Act lists together. No relation to the 1925 Geneva Protocol (AC-70) is coded here: any relationship is coded on the later instrument. No relation to the St Petersburg Declaration (AC-80) is coded: the preamble cites its sentiments only, and Renault stated that it implied no adhesion.

One row per signatory, accession and succession entry. Sweden and Norway and Austria-Hungary are historical rows without current status; the depositary's succession entries for Norway, Sweden, Austria and Hungary have their own rows. Montenegro (1878-1918) is coded from Trb. 1966, 232 and the 1905 Dutch list although the current depositary database and the ICRC omit it. The Kingdom of Serbia's 1899 signature and 1901 ratification are on a row linked to Serbia (historical), with the depositary's source label "Yugoslavia (< 25-06-1991)" preserved in its notes; the depositary's later succession entry "Serbia" (notified 7 September 2001, effective 27 April 1992) is a separate row. Germany, the Russian Federation, Türkiye and China keep the depositary's modern labels as a source-reporting convention, with the historical actor named in each row's notes and no continuity coded; Persia and Siam keep the names under which they signed. Current Status "State Party" is set only where the depositary database lists the entry without termination. Succession rows record the depositary's date of the succession act as Date of Succession and the date from which it takes effect as Entry into Force.
One row: a single prohibition binding all parties identically. The final clauses are procedural and appear in prose.
